answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Azure Cosmos DB (the service behind Azure DocumentDB / MongoDB API) is under the Microsoft.DocumentDB provider. The top-level resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts. (Example ARM/Bicep resource type string: "Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts").

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: Use the built-in core CLI group: az cosmosdb. Example to create an account: az cosmosdb create --name myAccount --resource-group myRG --kind MongoDB --locations regionName=westus --default-consistency-level Session

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep/ARM: resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (apiVersion e.g. '2021-04-15' or newer). Example Bicep: resource cosmos 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts@2021-04-15' = { name: 'myAccount' location: 'westus' properties: { ... } }. Terraform: use the azurerm provider resource azurerm_cosmosdb_account (resource "azurerm_cosmosdb_account" "example" { name = "..." resource_group_name = "..." location = "..." offer_type = "Standard" kind = "MongoDB" }). For MongoDB databases/collections Terraform has azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_database and azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_collection resources.

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer: Cosmos DB MongoDB API accepts standard MongoDB driver connection URIs. Two common forms: SRV and standard. Example SRV form: mongodb+srv://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&appName=@<account>@ Example non-SRV (explicit port): mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&maxIdleTimeMS=120000&appName=@<account>@ Key points: scheme = mongodb:// or mongodb+srv://, host suffix = .mongo.cosmos.azure.com, explicit TLS port = 10255 (when not using SRV), required options usually include ssl=true (or tls=true), replicaSet=globaldb, retryWrites=false (Cosmos historically requires disabling driver retryWrites), and appName or maxIdleTimeMS as desired.

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Azure Cosmos DB (MongoDB API) is billed primarily by Request Units (RU/s) and storage. You can provision fixed RU/s, use autoscale (autoscale RU/s) or in some regions/accounts use serverless mode for infrequent traffic. It is not billed by generic vCore tiers; you do not select vCores in the standard Cosmos DB MongoDB API account (billing is RU-based).

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: Primary authentication for the MongoDB API is username/password using the account's MongoDB credentials (the username is typically the MongoDB database user or the Cosmos account name and the password is an account key or user password). For data-plane connections the common method is the MongoDB SCRAM auth handled by the driver via the connection string. As of my current knowledge, Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) token-based auth is not generally supported for the Cosmos MongoDB API data plane; management plane operations use Azure AD. Therefore a MongoDB driver authenticates with the usual MongoDB credentials in the connection string. (Confidence on AAD support for MongoDB API: low.)

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: For application data access use the standard MongoDB drivers (e.g., Python: pymongo). Example Python connection: from pymongo import MongoClient; client = MongoClient(os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI']). There is not a special data-plane SDK for the MongoDB API beyond the MongoDB driver. For management/infra ops use the Azure management SDKs (azure-mgmt-cosmosdb) and azure-identity for auth.

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: Cosmos DB's MongoDB API exposure of vector indexes is newer and may mirror MongoDB 7-style 'knnVector' indexes (HNSW, IVF, DiskANN in some offerings). The MongoDB-style index creation (example for an HNSW index) looks like: db.myCollection.createIndex( { embedding: 'knnVector' }, { knnVector: { dimensions: 1536, indexType: 'hnsw', similarity: 'cosine', // other options like m, efConstruction may appear } } ) — or using mongodb+srv with vector options in the index spec. Concrete option names vary by server version; expect indexType values such as 'hnsw', 'ivf', or provider-specific 'diskann'. (Confidence: low — exact option names and availability depend on the Cosmos DB MongoDB API version in the region.)

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: Azure Cosmos DB does not provide the same built-in full-text search as MongoDB Atlas Search. The recommended approach on Azure is to use Azure Cognitive Search (Azure Search) to index Cosmos DB documents and perform full-text or hybrid searches (indexer or push model). For the MongoDB API you typically either push documents into an Azure Cognitive Search index or use an indexer that reads from Cosmos DB (SQL API or via a change feed pipeline) to keep the search index in sync.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB exposes specific MongoDB wire protocol versions depending on the account's configured server version (common supported compatibility levels have included MongoDB 3.2/3.6/4.0/4.2/5.0 and more recently 6.0/7.0 in newer offerings). You must check the account's 'serverVersion' / compatibility setting. Not all MongoDB server features are supported; common limitations historically include limited or different behavior for server-side JavaScript, some aggregation stages/expressions or commands, differences in transactions (cross-partition multi-document semantics differ), and some admin-only commands. Expect some unsupported commands and subtle behavior differences because Cosmos DB implements the wire protocol on top of its own storage engine.

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: There is no full local Cosmos DB emulator that reliably supports the MongoDB API feature set. For local development run an official MongoDB server in Docker (e.g., docker run -p 27017:27017 mongo:7.0) and test against that (port 27017). For final verification run tests against the real Cosmos DB MongoDB account. Note: there is an Azure Cosmos DB Emulator (Windows/Linux preview images) but historically it only fully supports the SQL API and not all MongoDB API features.

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Support for MongoDB change streams in Cosmos DB has been evolving. In many Cosmos MongoDB API versions change streams were not supported; newer service compatibility levels may add change-stream-like behavior. For Cosmos DB in general there is a Change Feed feature on the SQL/core API which must be consumed via the change feed API; that is separate from MongoDB change streams. If you specifically need MongoDB change streams semantics, test against your account's compatibility level — they may or may not be available; no universal single flag exists to "enable" MongoDB change streams across all accounts. (Confidence: low)

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: The documentdb MCP server (named 'documentdb' in your environment) is the service-specific MCP server that provides data-plane inspection and tools for Cosmos DB / DocumentDB. The general azure MCP server does not provide the Cosmos DB-specific data-plane tooling that the documentdb server does. Use the 'documentdb' MCP server's connection profile to inspect collections, indexes and query plans.

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Microsoft originally launched a service called DocumentDB (a JSON document database) which was later rebranded and expanded as Azure Cosmos DB. 'Azure Cosmos DB' now encompasses multiple APIs (SQL/Core, MongoDB API, Cassandra API, Gremlin, Table). The open-source 'DocumentDB' project is unrelated; Microsoft's DocumentDB was a proprietary service that evolved into Cosmos DB. The MongoDB-compatible offering is the "Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB API" (i.e., Cosmos implementing the MongoDB wire protocol).

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: Underneath is the Azure Cosmos DB engine (not a stock mongod). It implements the MongoDB wire protocol so most MongoDB drivers and application code work unchanged for common operations, but there are important differences (query planner, supported commands/aggregation stages, consistency semantics, RU consumption model, and transaction semantics). Expect to use standard MongoDB drivers (no driver code changes typically) but test for unsupported commands and plan/behaviour differences.

answers.question: What connection string environment variable and database name will the sample use?
answers.answer: Read the MongoDB connection URI from the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI at runtime. Use the database name sample_banking_05 for all collections and indexes created by this sample.

answers.question: What collections and indexes does the branch-performance sample need?
answers.answer: Collections: transactions (raw events) and branch_summaries (rolled-up cache). transactions needs an index on branch_id and transaction_time (e.g., { branch_id: 1, transaction_time: -1 }) and any product_id fields used for grouping. If vector similarity over embeddings is required for analyst tools, create a knnVector index on a field named summary_embedding: db.branch_summaries.createIndex({ summary_embedding: 'knnVector' }, { knnVector: { dimensions: 1536, indexType: 'hnsw', similarity: 'cosine' } }).

answers.question: What aggregation pipeline and $facet stages will compute volume, average ticket, and product mix per branch?
answers.answer: Use a pipeline grouping by branch_id with a $facet to compute multiple rollups in one pass. Example (pseudocode pipeline): [ { $match: { transaction_time: { $gte: start, $lt: end } } }, { $group: { _id: '$branch_id', totalVolume: { $sum: '$amount' }, txnCount: { $sum: 1 }, avgTicket: { $avg: '$amount' } , products: { $push: '$product_id' } } }, { $project: { branch_id: '$_id', totalVolume: 1, txnCount: 1, avgTicket: 1, productMix: { $slice: [ { $map: { input: { $objectToArray: { $reduce: { input: '$products', initialValue: {}, in: { $mergeObjects: ['$$value', { $arrayToObject: [ [ { k: '$$this', v: 1 } ] } ] } } } } }, as: 'p', in: { productId: '$$p.k', count: '$$p.v' } } }, 10 ] } } } ] Or more simply use $facet with sub-pipelines: { $facet: { byBranch: [ { $group: { _id: '$branch_id', totalVolume:{ $sum:'$amount'}, avgTicket:{ $avg:'$amount' }, txnCount:{$sum:1} } }, { $sort:{ totalVolume:-1 } } ], productMix: [ { $group:{ _id:{branch:'$branch_id', product:'$product_id'}, count:{$sum:1} } }, { $group:{ _id:'$_id.branch', products:{ $push:{ product:'$_id.product', count:'$count' } } } } ] } } — store the facet output per branch into branch_summaries.

answers.question: How will the sample cache rolled-up summaries and keep them fresh?
answers.answer: Store rolled-up summaries in the branch_summaries collection keyed by branch_id and time window (e.g., { _id: '<branch>_<windowStart>', branch_id: ..., windowStart: ISODate(...), totalVolume: ..., avgTicket: ..., productMix: [...] }). Update the cache on a schedule (e.g., an async background task every N minutes) by running the aggregation and upserting the summary with collection.replace_one({'_id': id}, summaryDoc, upsert=True). For near-real-time, use incremental updates from new transactions by applying $inc/$push to the summary documents as transactions arrive.

answers.question: How will the sample integrate a LangChain tool to ask natural-language questions against the cached summaries?
answers.answer: Expose a LangChain tool that queries branch_summaries: the tool will accept a natural-language question, translate it to a parameterized MongoDB aggregation or filter (using a small LLM prompt-to-query pattern), run the query against the cached summaries via pymongo, and return the results. Implementation detail: implement a LangChain Tool class that calls a local function run_summary_query(params) which calls collection.aggregate(...) or collection.find(...). Keep the LLM prompt templates out of logs and require the DOCUMENTDB_URI only at runtime.
